permits.name: Form your legal entity with the NY Department of State (LLC / corporation)
permits.issuing_agency: New York Department of State – Division of Corporations
permits.notes: LLC Articles of Organization cost $200; online filings are acknowledged by email within minutes, and optional expedited handling is $25 (24 hours), $75 (same day) or $150 (2 hours). Do this first: the EIN, sales tax Certificate of Authority, lease and SLA application all need the exact entity name. LLCs then owe the separate publication requirement (see next item).

permits.name: LLC publication requirement + Certificate of Publication
permits.issuing_agency: New York Department of State – Division of Corporations (newspapers designated by the county clerk)
permits.notes: Within 120 days of forming, an LLC must publish a notice of formation in two newspapers designated by the county clerk, then file the Certificate of Publication with the affidavits ($50 state fee). Newspaper charges are the real cost: a few hundred dollars upstate, but often $1,000–$2,000 in New York County (Manhattan). If you miss the deadline, the LLC's authority to do business is suspended until you publish and file. Corporations and sole proprietors can skip this item.
permits.stall_risk: Operators forget the 120-day window and find their LLC suspended when a bank, landlord or the SLA checks status. Order publication through a service the week the LLC is formed; in Manhattan, ask the county clerk which papers are designated and get quotes, since prices vary widely.

permits.name: NYS Sales Tax Certificate of Authority
permits.issuing_agency: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance (via NY Business Express)
permits.notes: You must register with the Tax Department at least 20 days before you begin business, and you cannot legally make taxable sales (prepared food, drinks, hotel rooms) until the certificate arrives. Register online through New York Business Express with a NY.gov Business account. Operating without one carries penalties of up to $500 for the first day and $200 for each day after, up to $10,000. The SLA and NYC Health Department both ask for the certificate.

permits.name: Register as an employer with NYS DOL (unemployment insurance; NYS-45 quarterly filer)
permits.issuing_agency: New York State Department of Labor – Unemployment Insurance Division
permits.notes: General business employers become liable for unemployment insurance on the first day of the quarter in which they pay $300 or more in wages. Register online through New York Business Express (form NYS-100 by mail for non-profits) to get your UI employer number, then file the combined NYS-45 withholding/wage/UI return every quarter through the Tax Department. Your payroll provider needs the account number before the first pay run.

permits.name: Workers' compensation insurance
permits.issuing_agency: Any licensed carrier or NYS Insurance Fund (regulated by the NYS Workers' Compensation Board)
permits.notes: Virtually every New York employer must carry workers' comp from the first employee and post the notice of coverage. Premiums are a percentage of payroll, not a fee. NYC agencies (Health Department, DCWP) and the SLA ask for proof of coverage (form C-105.2 or the CE-200 exemption) with your application, so bind a policy before you file those.

permits.name: Disability benefits (DBL) + Paid Family Leave insurance
permits.issuing_agency: Licensed carrier or NYS Insurance Fund (regulated by the NYS Workers' Compensation Board)
permits.notes: New York is one of the few states where short-term disability coverage is mandatory: once you have had one or more employees on 30 days in a calendar year, coverage must start four weeks later, and Paid Family Leave is added as a rider to the same policy. Employers may withhold a small employee contribution. Buy it with the workers' comp policy; the same carrier usually quotes both.

permits.name: 30-day advance notice to the municipality / Community Board (SLA on-premises applications)
permits.issuing_agency: NYS Liquor Authority (notice delivered to the city/town/village clerk, or the Community Board in NYC)
permits.notes: Applicants for on-premises licenses must notify the local municipality at least 30 days before filing with the SLA; in New York City the notice goes to the Community Board for the premises. Delivery is by certified mail, overnight delivery or personal service (email only where the board has opted in), and you must keep proof to attach to the SLA application. The 30-day clock is pure wait time, so send the notice as soon as the lease is signed.

permits.name: SLA On-Premises Liquor license (OP 252) – full bar in a restaurant, bar or hotel
permits.notes: Two-year license: $4,352 in New York, Kings, Bronx and Queens counties ($3,072 Richmond and large upstate cities, $1,792 elsewhere) plus a $200 non-refundable filing fee. Hotels file the Hotel Liquor (HL 242) class and caterers the Catering Establishment class through the same SLA Application Wizard. Restaurants must serve full meals with a kitchen; the 200-foot rule bars OP licenses on the same street within 200 feet of a school or place of worship. Ask for a Temporary Retail Permit with the application if the landlord timeline is tight.
permits.stall_risk: In NYC, processing commonly runs 4–8 months once Community Board review and any 500-foot hearing are included. Make the lease contingent on SLA approval, file a complete application (incomplete files go to the back of the queue), and request a temporary retail permit.

permits.name: SLA Restaurant Wine license (RW 341) – beer, wine and cider in a restaurant
permits.notes: Two-year license: $960 in the NYC counties and large cities, $480 elsewhere, plus a $100 filing fee. Covers beer, cider, mead and wine for a premises operated as a restaurant serving full meals. Beer- and wine-only licenses are exempt from both the 200-foot and the 500-foot rules, which is why many NYC restaurants open with an RW and upgrade to OP later. Hotels use the equivalent Hotel Wine (HW) class at the same fee.

permits.name: SLA Tavern Wine license (TW 344) – beer and wine bar without a full kitchen
permits.notes: Two-year license: $1,152 in the NYC counties and large cities, $540 elsewhere, plus a $100 filing fee. For wine bars, beer bars and taprooms that have a food-prep area but are not full restaurants; no liquor. Like other beer/wine classes it is exempt from the 500-foot rule, but in NYC the Community Board still reviews it and often asks for stipulations on hours and music.

permits.name: SLA Eating Place Beer license (EB 141) – beer and cider only
permits.notes: Three-year license: $960 in the NYC counties and large cities, $480 elsewhere, plus a $100 filing fee. Allows beer, cider and mead at any place that serves food for on-premises consumption, which suits cafes, pizzerias and counter-service spots. If you also want wine, apply for Restaurant Wine (RW) instead; the fee is the same but the term is two years.

permits.name: SLA 500-foot rule public-interest hearing (new full-liquor premises)
permits.notes: In municipalities over 20,000 people the SLA cannot issue an on-premises liquor license within 500 feet of three or more existing on-premises liquor licensees unless it holds a hearing and finds the license is in the public interest. Applicants must post the hearing notice at the entrance within 10 days of receiving it; community testimony carries weight. Beer and wine licenses are exempt. Check the SLA's public license query for nearby OP licenses before signing a lease.
permits.stall_risk: Dense nightlife blocks (Lower East Side, East Village, Williamsburg) almost always trigger the hearing, and opposition can lead to denial or heavy conditions. Budget 2–4 extra months, bring a detailed method of operation, and consider launching with a beer/wine license.

permits.name: Alcohol Training Awareness Program (ATAP) for servers (voluntary)
permits.notes: Not mandatory in New York, but the SLA recommends it for every licensee and server, and proof of staff training can reduce the penalty if you are charged with a violation such as a sale to a minor. Courses from SLA-certified schools take a few hours online or in person. Community Boards frequently write ATAP training into license stipulations.
